segments.text: Most software we use every day, like a calculator or a spreadsheet, is built on a specific foundation.
But to understand AI, we have to look at how it's built on something else entirely.
In normal software, human programmers write exact, line-by-line code.
These instructions tell the software exactly what to do in every situation.
This flowchart shows the core of normal software—rules.
The most common type is an if-then-else statement.
When a user enters a password, the rule checks it.
If it matches, then the app opens.
Else, it shows an error.
Written rules return the same result every time.
AI works differently.
Programmers don't write rules for every possible situation.
Instead, the software relies on patterns it absorbed during its training.
On the left, the model digests massive data to convert examples into numerical patterns.
On the right, AI uses probability to score possible next words based on what's written so far.
It predicts the likely next word, adds it, and runs the process again.
Learn patterns first. Build every answer.
To visualize this, think of normal software as a robot following a recipe in a cookbook.
Someone wrote every step, and the robot follows the rules to make the exact same dish every time.
AI is more like a chef.
No one handed it a cookbook, but because it has cooked thousands of meals, it recognizes the patterns.
It can handle a dish it's never made before, changing how the software solves problems—and how it fails.
We can see this difference in action by asking both types of software the same question.
What's the best game for my new PS5?
Normal software follows a fixed rule, showing the top game on a preset list.
It repeats Marvel's Spider-Man 2 every single time you ask.
On the right, AI builds a fresh response using patterns.
Asking the same question yields different recommendations.
Rules repeat the programmed answer.
Patterns build a fresh one.
This pattern recognition also changes how the software handles the information you feed it.
Normal software requires structured data, like entering grades into specific rows and columns in a spreadsheet.
This graphic compares the two.
AI handles unstructured data, messy information like scribbles on a receipt, and transforms it into an organized table.
For example, the messy scribbled notes for this video were turned into a coherent first draft.
You bring the mess, AI helps make sense of it.
For exact, consistent tasks like checking a password, normal software is the right tool.
But AI is built for the messy, open-ended jobs that rules can't cover.
While a human carries kryptonite in a backpack, it's dangerous for Superman.
AI has its own critical weaknesses that we need to be aware of.
This infographic shows why.
Because AI uses probabilistic patterns rather than rules, it's inherently harder to control.
Trained behavior is harder to predict, inspect, and lock down.
These unpredictable patterns can lead to scams that scale, humiliating deepfakes, or answers that sound correct even when flat wrong.
During training, they teach AI to avoid harmful behavior.
They also add a safety layer to the apps, guardrails.
These block or redirect harmful requests, but they aren't perfect.
They can miss something dangerous or block something harmless.
As we have seen, AI's foundation gives it exciting new superpowers.
But those superpowers come with kryptonite.
